notice: Original synthetic teaching documents for offline demonstration. These are not web search results and do not establish facts about any actual market, company, user population, or product.

documents.title: DEMO fixture: Customer discovery and product validation
documents.content: DEMO TEACHING FIXTURE. This is an original synthetic product research exercise, not a report about real customers. In this exercise, a student founder writes a problem statement, identifies target users, and records assumptions before building a startup prototype. Customer discovery interviews ask about a recent concrete experience with the problem, the current workaround, and the time or effort involved. A proposed app, assistant, platform, education tool, or service remains an untested idea until users test it. The exercise separates what a user said from what the founder inferred. Product validation uses a small task-based prototype and records whether users complete the task. Synthetic sample statistic for testing quantity extraction: 12 simulated interview records include 7 simulated respondents interested in trying the exercise prototype. These numbers are invented teaching data, not real interviews or market validation. Evidence from this fixture supports the exercise process only. It provides no evidence that any particular startup has demand, paying users, adoption, or revenue. Market size and willingness to pay must remain unknown until relevant external research and user evidence are collected.

documents.title: DEMO fixture: Competitor research worksheet
documents.content: DEMO TEACHING FIXTURE. This is an original synthetic competitor research worksheet, not a review of actual companies. For a startup app idea, record the alternatives that target users could use to solve the same problem. Alternatives may include manual work, an existing workflow, a general software tool, or a specialist service. Each comparison needs a source URL, a retrieval date, and evidence for any stated product feature or price. A competitor feature or pricing assumption is not verified merely because it sounds plausible. A proposed difference in a student prototype can be described as a design intention. The exercise asks the founder to compare the problem solved, target users, onboarding steps, data requirements, and output quality. It does not name real competitors or establish a product's unique position. Current competitor features, pricing, and market trends require live research.

documents.title: DEMO fixture: Prototype feasibility and scope
documents.content: DEMO TEACHING FIXTURE. This original synthetic exercise outlines prototype feasibility checks for a student startup app and AI assistant. A prototype scope names the smallest complete user task, required inputs, output format, and test criteria. The development exercise can evaluate a web frontend, a backend API, document storage, an AI model provider, retrieval, and a clear error state. Development feasibility depends on data access, available API accounts, model performance, implementation time, and reliable integration between modules. Mock data can demonstrate software behavior while live model and research services are unavailable. A mock run cannot establish the quality of a live AI system. Synthetic sample budget for testing quantity extraction: the hypothetical classroom pilot has a budget of INR 5000 and a duration of 4 weeks. These amounts and durations are invented teaching data, not provider prices, a real startup budget, or a feasibility estimate. For a GenAI workflow, structured outputs and source references help modules share one consistent project context. Actual model latency, accuracy, cost, and commercial feasibility remain unknown without measurements from a configured live system.

documents.title: DEMO fixture: Evidence grounding and AI critic
documents.content: DEMO TEACHING FIXTURE. This original synthetic exercise explains evidence grounding in a student AI startup research prototype. Search results are source material; retrieved excerpts are evidence; a model-generated analysis is a separate output. Each evidence excerpt has a source identifier and a locator. A supported factual claim needs relevant evidence, not simply an attached citation. Assumptions should be explicitly marked and missing evidence should remain a gap. A second AI critic checks unsupported market claims, contradictions, missing target-user detail, weak competitor comparisons, and ambiguous feasibility statements. The critic can recommend one revision pass; it cannot prove that the first model is correct. Retrieval should preserve source text and allow a reader to inspect its origin. In this demonstration, synthetic fixtures can support statements about this teaching exercise only. They cannot validate a real startup business idea, prove market demand, or justify a real competitive advantage.

documents.title: DEMO fixture: Prototype risks and evaluation
documents.content: DEMO TEACHING FIXTURE. This original synthetic worksheet covers prototype evaluation for a student startup product, platform, or AI app. The exercise asks the team to list risks as hypotheses to test: low user adoption, uncertain demand, unavailable data, incorrect AI claims, expensive provider usage, and fragile integrations. These are possible risks, not measured failures of any real project. Each proposed mitigation has an owner and a practical validation task. The evaluation worksheet records extraction completeness, source-reference correctness, evidence relevance, analysis uncertainty, critic findings, and successful handoff of the shared project context. A tested export is evidence that a file is structurally usable, not proof of business viability. No actual market statistics, production reliability numbers, user interview results, or model quality scores are provided by this fixture.
